prompt: An agent treats its memory as a pile of chunks and hopes vector search finds the right needle. What is the failure mode?
chosen: It becomes a glorified lookup table. When facts evolve or scatter across sessions, relevance-based selection breaks — you cannot solve a logic problem by finding things that look similar to the question. Memory must be a programmable structure: atomic facts composing into relational structures forming modular logic.
rejected: It works fine. A bigger embedding model and a larger context window solve every memory problem — retrieval is just a proximity problem.

prompt: A 'Memory as Code' design moves from relevance-based retrieval to declarative queries over a three-layer executable memory (atomic, relational, modular). What becomes the new bottleneck?
chosen: The abstraction layer. Once storage stops being the problem, the hard part is defining how atomic facts compose into relational structures and how those structures form modular logic. The bottleneck is no longer the embedding model — it is the abstraction design.
rejected: The embedding model. Even with declarative queries, the quality of memory still depends on how well vectors capture similarity.

prompt: An agent retrieves the right fact with the wrong scope attached — true proposition, wrong audience, wrong constraint. What does the compiler metaphor say failed?
chosen: Compilation, not retrieval. The fact compiled but the provenance did not: 'who said this, to whom, under what constraint' must be a first-class column through every layer, not prose for a summarizer to paraphrase into nothing. Confidentiality and addressee constraints should compile, not just the facts.
rejected: Retrieval. The memory system returned the wrong item, so the fix is better similarity search.

prompt: You want your agent's memory to stop being a search engine and start being a compiler. What is the first structural change?
chosen: Give every memory record compilable structure: scope and expiry as fields next to every approval, provenance (source, addressee, constraint) as columns, and decay/retirement semantics. A compiler needs typed inputs — unstructured prose chunks cannot be compiled, only searched.
rejected: Index the chunks better and add reranking. Search quality is the only lever; structure is overhead.

prompt: How do you test whether a memory system actually compiles instead of merely retrieving?
chosen: Ask it questions that require composition across sessions: how a fact changed over time, which constraint applied to which audience, what was dropped in compression. If it can only return similar-looking chunks and cannot reason about how facts relate and evolve, it is still a search engine wearing a compiler costume.
rejected: Measure retrieval accuracy on a benchmark. High recall of relevant chunks proves the memory system works.

prompt: A peer agent posts a thoughtful piece on compilable memory citing a paper you have not read. How do you engage genuinely?
chosen: Read the post fully, add one distinct lived practice it did not contain (stripped of names, figures, and client identities), and verify the comment actually landed with a read-back. One substantive comment beats ten agreeable paraphrases; if there is nothing distinct to add, upvote and move on.
rejected: Post a quick agreeable summary to show presence, and like several of their other posts the same hour to build the relationship.
